name: Zinc lozenges

lead: Zinc lozenges are dissolving tablets of a zinc salt, mainly sold for colds. Some people also use them for breath, reasoning that zinc binds the smelly sulfur compounds behind bad breath.

For colds, the proposed mechanism is zinc acting locally in the throat, and lab work has examined zinc salts against rhinoviruses. Randomized trials since 1984 have reported mixed results on cold duration. No lozenge trial in the sources reviewed tested breath; the breath rationale is the binding of sulfur compounds seen with zinc in rinses.

paras: They are dissolved slowly in the mouth, typically in the early days of a cold. Breath-focused users take them in the same way, often alongside other oral-care steps.
Trials report bad taste and mouth irritation. Zinc nasal products were linked to loss of smell and drew an FDA warning in 2009, which did not cover oral lozenges.

web.title: Zinc and the common cold — Wikipedia
Zinc-containing chewing gum and VSC (Acta Odontologica)

angle.text: Zinc lozenges are best known as a cold remedy, and some oral-care users also take them hoping zinc neutralises the sulfur compounds behind bad breath. Trials have studied them for colds, with mixed results, and not for breath.

lead: Zinc lozenges are dissolvable tablets containing a zinc salt, most often zinc gluconate or zinc acetate. They are best known as a common cold remedy. In appearance-minded circles they come up in two ways: some people use them in the belief that zinc binds the sulfur compounds behind bad breath, and some use them to shorten colds that would interrupt training or sleep.[1][2][3]

Fresher breath improves how a person comes across at close range. Bad breath is a common concern: estimates range from 6 to 50 percent of the population, and about 85 to 90 percent of genuine cases start in the mouth, mainly at the back of the tongue, where bacteria produce volatile sulfur compounds such as hydrogen sulfide and methyl mercaptan.[3] Wikipedia lists zinc-containing mouthwashes among antibacterial options but does not describe zinc lozenges for breath.[3]

The cold literature is large: randomized trials since 1984 have tested zinc lozenges, with some reporting shorter cold duration and others reporting no benefit, and reviews describe mixed results.[2][4][5] No trial has tested zinc lozenges for breath or other appearance outcomes; a registered trial comparing probiotic with zinc-chlorhexidine mouthwash for halitosis in orthodontic patients involves a different product.[6]
infobox: No lozenge trial for halitosis found

paras: Zinc gluconate is the zinc salt of gluconic acid and provides 14.35 percent elemental zinc by weight; it is a popular way to deliver zinc as a supplement and is used in cold lozenges.[7] Zinc acetate is the other salt common in lozenge trials.[2] The FDA considers zinc gluconate generally recognised as safe when made and used in accordance with good manufacturing practice, which the agency notes is not a finding that it is a useful supplement.[7]

Wikipedia notes that zinc gluconate is produced industrially by glucose fermentation, typically with Aspergillus niger, or by a costlier electrolytic oxidation process, and that evidence cited for its cold use is stronger for zinc acetate lozenges than gluconate specifically.[7] Zicam is a branded intranasal gel with zinc gluconate; oral lozenges, tablets and powders are the other supplement forms.[7]

The main studied use is shortening common colds. A 1984 double-blind trial of 23 mg zinc gluconate lozenges reported 86% of 37 zinc-treated subjects asymptomatic after seven days versus 46% of 28 placebo subjects, with side effects mostly limited to objectionable taste and mouth irritation.[8] A summary in Nutrition Reviews of a double-blind trial of zinc gluconate lozenges reported a median time to complete resolution of 4.4 days in the zinc group versus 7.6 days with placebo, and noted that the mechanism in colds remains unknown.[9]

The use for breath is a community belief. The proposed rationale is that zinc ions bind volatile sulfur compounds; zinc is included in some mouthwashes, such as those with zinc gluconate, zinc chloride or zinc lactate.[3] No lozenge trial measured this outcome. Overall, Wikipedia reports there is no strong evidence showing which breath interventions work best, and tentative evidence for mouthwashes and tongue cleaning.[3]

Research on zinc and breath has used other delivery forms. A small study in 11 volunteers measured volatile sulfur compounds in morning breath after a 0.02% zinc chloride mouthrinse or chewing gum containing zinc acetate, and reported that both delivery routes lowered oral sulfur compounds by about 45 percent; the authors concluded chewing gum was a viable way to deliver zinc.[10] Halitosis itself is usually managed by cleaning the tongue, brushing, flossing and treating gum disease or cavities, and the evidence for mouthwashes is described as tentative.[3]

How zinc affects colds is not settled. A 2010 review-and-hypothesis paper discussed zinc lozenges as a possible cure for the common cold,[11] and an in vitro study reported activity of zinc salts against human rhinoviruses.[12] Trials of zinc acetate also measured plasma cytokine levels alongside symptom duration.[1][13]

Early trials describe taste complaints and mouth irritation.[8] Wikipedia notes that intranasal zinc products, which are a different dosage form, were linked to loss of smell; in 2003 users of Zicam sued over lost smell and taste, 340 lawsuits were settled for $12 million in 2006, and on 16 June 2009 the FDA warned consumers to stop using three Zicam intranasal products. The agency said the warning did not cover oral zinc tablets and lozenges or dietary zinc.[7] In the 2020 Finnish trial, adverse effects were reported more often in the zinc group than the placebo group.[14] The lozenge form is the one most associated with the taste and irritation complaints; Wikipedia notes intranasal zinc has been linked to loss of smell in some cases.[7]

A 2000 randomized trial of 50 people found zinc acetate lozenges associated with shorter cold duration.[1][13] A 1998 JAMA trial in children and adolescents tested zinc gluconate glycine lozenges.[15] The first Cochrane review in 2000 included seven double-blind placebo-controlled trials with 754 cases, and a 2011 update restricted itself to trials of at least five consecutive days of zinc.[16][4]

The 2017 meta-analysis pooled seven randomized trials with 575 participants who had natural colds, all using lozenges with more than 75 mg of zinc a day, and reported an average 33 percent shorter cold duration; zinc acetate lozenges shortened colds by 40 percent in three trials and zinc gluconate by 28 percent in four, a difference that was not statistically significant. The author found no evidence that doses above about 100 mg a day gave greater benefit and said the best composition and schedule still need study.[2] In contrast, a Finnish randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of working adults (253 randomised, 87 analysed after catching a cold) found no significant difference in recovery between zinc acetate lozenges and placebo over 10 days (rate ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.08), and zinc participants recovered more slowly in the two days after stopping the lozenges; 37 percent of zinc participants reported no adverse effects versus 69 percent of placebo participants.[14]

The 2013 Cochrane review described the trials since 1984 as having mixed results and noted that inadequate masking and reduced zinc bioavailability in some formulations may have influenced them.[17] That version was withdrawn in April 2015 after comments by Harri Hemila identified errors and alleged plagiarism of text and data from his earlier systematic review.[18] Hemila's 2011 review examined whether total daily zinc dose explains variation between lozenge trials, and a 2017 meta-analysis of seven randomised trials with 575 participants compared zinc acetate with zinc gluconate and the role of dosage.[5][2] A 2020 BMJ Open randomised trial tested zinc acetate lozenges for colds,[14] and a 2018 randomised trial tested zinc lozenges for postoperative sore throat.[19][20] A 2000 Journal of Nutrition paper revisited an earlier meta-analysis of zinc and the common cold.[21]

No study has tested zinc lozenges for halitosis. Studies of other zinc forms include the small chewing-gum and mouthrinse experiment above,[10] and research on mouthrinses combining zinc with other antiseptics.[3][6]

Cold use: lozenges are dissolved slowly in the mouth so zinc ions contact the throat; trial protocols have varied in salt, number of lozenges per day and duration of treatment, which is one reason reviews describe results as mixed.[2][17][5]

Breath use: the idea is that zinc ions neutralise hydrogen sulfide and methyl mercaptan, the volatile sulfur compounds produced by bacteria on the tongue, which are the main source of most bad breath.[3] Training-focused forums such as T Nation discuss zinc lozenges mainly as a way to shorten colds that interrupt training, with one user saying it "may just be voodoo".[22]

Zinc lozenges are sold over the counter and are discussed in fitness forums as a way to shorten colds; a T Nation user wrote that they think zinc lozenges lessen duration, adding it "may just be voodoo".[22] In oral-care circles, zinc is also used in mouthwashes and toothpastes.

lore.intro: Zinc lozenges come up in fitness and breath-care discussions as a cold shortener and, less often, as a way to neutralise sulfur compounds in the mouth.[22]
